newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Garuda must cut deficit before flotation - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Garuda must cut deficit before flotation - analysts.

text.p: Indonesia's national air carrier, Garuda Indonesia, must improve its financial performance before the government can float it on the Jakarta Stock Exchange, analysts said on Thursday.

Trade Minister Haryanto Dhanutirto told parliament on Monday Garuda had suffered first-half 1996 losses of 2.65 billion rupiah ($1.14 million) after reporting a profit of 135.79 billion rupiah ($58.5 million) in the 1995 calendar year.

"If Garuda still plans to float shares on the stock exchange, they will first have to improve efficiency and prove it by their financial performance," Christianto Wibisono, director of Indonesia Data Business Centre, told Reuters.
Garuda would have to improve its efficiency before it could expect to write off its debt and get further financial injections from the government, Wibisono said.
"It will still be two to three years before Garuda is privatised because its financial position is still very weak," he added.
The government has said it plans to float Garuda in 1998.
Garuda was not immediately able to give reasons for the first-half loss. There were no comparative figures for the first six months of last year.
"We have not yet had our results audited by the State Audit Board and until the audited results are published I cannot give more detailed figures," Garuda spokesman Arief Hartanto said.
"In general, this deficit will definitely affect Garuda's plans for privitisation," an analyst with a foreign security house said.
Asked if the government should wait until Garuda reduced its losses before injecting further money, he said: "Definitely".
Garuda's debt was almost five times equity in early 1996. A government takeover of debt worth $745 million in May was necessary to replenish the airline's balance sheet.
In the long term, the privatisation of Garuda is crucial to improving its financial position through increased accountability, Wibisono said.
"Besides raising fresh funds from the public, privatisation will make Garuda realise it cannot rely on a monopoly situation anymore and should improve its competitiveness," he said.

The government has listed four state-owned companies on the Jakarta bourse since July 1991. They are cement maker PT Semen Gresik, satellite operator PT Indonesia Satellite Corp, telecommunications company PT Telekomunikasi Indonesia and tin producer PT Tambang Timah.
Other state-owned companies the government has said it plans to list include Bank Negara Indonesia (BNI), toll-road operator Jasa Marga and steel producer Krakatau Steel.
Local media reports have said Garuda planned to split from its subsidiary Merpati Nusantara Airlines later this year to boost the performance of both companies.
Garuda operates 59 planes, including Boeing, Airbus and McDonnell Douglas jetliners which serve regional and international routes.
